original_abstract: Omnidirectional scene text detection has received increasing research attention. Previous methods directly predict words or text lines of quadrilateral shapes. However, most methods neglect the significance of consistent labeling, which is important to maintain a stable training process, especially when a large amount of data are included. For the first time, we solve the problem in this paper by proposing a novel method termed Sequential-free Box Discretization (SBD). The proposed SBD first discretizes the quadrilateral box into several key edges, which contains all potential horizontal and vertical positions. In order to decode accurate vertex positions, a simple yet effective matching procedure is proposed to reconstruct the quadrilateral bounding boxes. It departs from the learning ambiguity which has a significant influence during the learning process. Exhaustive ablation studies have been conducted to quantitatively validate the effectiveness of our proposed method. More importantly, built upon SBD, we provide a detailed analysis of the impact of a collection of refinements, in the hope to inspire others to build state-of-the-art networks. Combining both SBD and these useful refinements, we achieve state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks, including ICDAR 2015, and MLT. Our method also wins the first place in text detection task of the recent ICDAR2019 Robust Reading Challenge on Reading Chinese Text on Signboard, further demonstrating its powerful generalization ability. Code is available at this https URL.
generated_abstract: Scene text detection remains a challenging task due to the arbitrary orientations, varying aspect ratios, and small sizes of text in natural images. While existing methods have made significant progress, they often rely on complex pipelines or post-processing steps that limit efficiency and accuracy. This paper introduces a novel approach that directly addresses these challenges through an end-to-end framework designed for fast and accurate detection of arbitrarily oriented text. By integrating efficient boundary regression and adaptive region representation, our method eliminates the need for intermediate steps such as candidate aggregation or post-processing, enabling real-time performance. The proposed framework is evaluated on multiple benchmarks, demonstrating superior accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. Experimental results show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard datasets, including ICDAR 2015 and COCO-Text, with high F-measure scores and fast inference speeds. The method also shows strong adaptability to irregularly shaped text, making it suitable for a wide range of real-world applications.

original_abstract: Conventional cross-domain image-to-image translation or unsupervised domain adaptation methods assume that the source domain and target domain are closely related. This neglects a practical scenario where the domain discrepancy between the source and target is excessively large. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to learn domain adaptive features between the largely-gapped source and target domains with unlabeled domain bridges. Firstly, we introduce the framework of Cycle-consistency Flow Generative Adversarial Networks (CFGAN) that utilizes domain bridges to perform image-to-image translation between two distantly distributed domains. Secondly, we propose the Prototypical Adversarial Domain Adaptation (PADA) model which utilizes unlabeled bridge domains to align feature distribution between source and target with a large discrepancy. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed models.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of adapting deep models from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain, where the distributions of the two domains differ significantly. Building on prior work that leverages adversarial learning, feature alignment, and moment matching, we propose a novel approach that integrates domain-invariant feature learning with task-specific decision boundary alignment. Our method avoids generating ambiguous features near class boundaries by incorporating feedback from classifiers trained on the source domain. It dynamically aligns feature distributions across domains while preserving discriminative information necessary for downstream tasks. The approach is implemented using standard deep learning components and can be trained efficiently with backpropagation. Experiments on standard image classification and segmentation benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves competitive performance, effectively bridging the domain gap without requiring labeled target data. The results suggest that aligning task-specific decision boundaries enhances adaptation performance, particularly in scenarios with large domain shifts.

original_abstract: The revolution in computer hardware, especially in graphics processing units and tensor processing units, has enabled significant advances in computer graphics and artificial intelligence algorithms. In addition to their many beneficial applications in daily life and business, computer-generated/manipulated images and videos can be used for malicious purposes that violate security systems, privacy, and social trust. The deepfake phenomenon and its variations enable a normal user to use his or her personal computer to easily create fake videos of anybody from a short real online video. Several countermeasures have been introduced to deal with attacks using such videos. However, most of them are targeted at certain domains and are ineffective when applied to other domains or new attacks. In this paper, we introduce a capsule network that can detect various kinds of attacks, from presentation attacks using printed images and replayed videos to attacks using fake videos created using deep learning. It uses many fewer parameters than traditional convolutional neural networks with similar performance. Moreover, we explain, for the first time ever in the literature, the theory behind the application of capsule networks to the forensics problem through detailed analysis and visualization.
generated_abstract: The proliferation of synthetic media has introduced significant challenges in distinguishing between authentic and manipulated facial content, particularly in video formats. While prior work has focused on detecting such manipulations in still images or using single-task approaches, the temporal dynamics of video streams and the need for simultaneous detection and localization of tampered regions remain underexplored. Building on recent advances in deep learning and multi-task frameworks, we propose a novel approach that integrates temporal modeling with joint detection and segmentation of manipulated facial content in videos. Our method leverages recurrent convolutional strategies to exploit temporal coherence and employs a multi-task learning architecture to simultaneously identify forged content and delineate manipulated regions. Experiments on the FaceForensics++ dataset demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in both detection and segmentation tasks, while maintaining robustness to compression and varying attack types. These results highlight the effectiveness of combining temporal modeling with multi-task learning for enhanced video-based facial forgery detection.

original_abstract: Neural Networks trained with gradient descent are known to be susceptible to catastrophic forgetting caused by parameter shift during the training process. In the context of Neural Machine Translation (NMT) this results in poor performance on heterogeneous datasets and on sub-tasks like rare phrase translation. On the other hand, non-parametric approaches are immune to forgetting, perfectly complementing the generalization ability of NMT. However, attempts to combine non-parametric or retrieval based approaches with NMT have only been successful on narrow domains, possibly due to over-reliance on sentence level retrieval. We propose a novel n-gram level retrieval approach that relies on local phrase level similarities, allowing us to retrieve neighbors that are useful for translation even when overall sentence similarity is low. We complement this with an expressive neural network, allowing our model to extract information from the noisy retrieved context. We evaluate our semi-parametric NMT approach on a heterogeneous dataset composed of WMT, IWSLT, JRC-Acquis and OpenSubtitles, and demonstrate gains on all 4 evaluation sets. The semi-parametric nature of our approach opens the door for non-parametric domain adaptation, demonstrating strong inference-time adaptation performance on new domains without the need for any parameter updates.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of improving the adequacy of neural machine translation (NMT) systems, which often struggle to capture the full meaning of source sentences compared to statistical machine translation (SMT). Building on prior work that explores hybrid approaches combining NMT with SMT features, phrase-based models, and retrieval-based methods, we propose a novel framework that integrates multiple sources of linguistic knowledge into the NMT decoding process. Our approach leverages both phrase-based translation probabilities and retrieved translation examples to guide the NMT model during inference. By incorporating these external signals, we aim to enhance the model's ability to recall and appropriately translate low-frequency words and phrases, as well as improve the overall fluency and accuracy of translations. Experimental results on multiple language pairs demonstrate that our method leads to significant improvements in translation quality, as measured by BLEU scores, while maintaining computational efficiency. These findings suggest that combining the strengths of different translation paradigms can yield more robust and effective NMT systems.

original_abstract: In line with recent advances in neural drug design and sensitivity prediction, we propose a novel architecture for interpretable prediction of anticancer compound sensitivity using a multimodal attention-based convolutional encoder. Our model is based on the three key pillars of drug sensitivity: compounds’ structure in the form of a SMILES sequence, gene expression profiles of tumors and prior knowledge on intracellular interactions from protein-protein interaction networks. We demonstrate that our multiscale convolutional attention-based encoder significantly outperforms a baseline model trained on Morgan fingerprints, a selection of encoders based on SMILES as well as previously reported state of the art for multimodal drug sensitivity prediction (R2 = 0.86 and RMSE = 0.89). Moreover, the explainability of our approach is demonstrated by a thorough analysis of the attention weights. generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of accurately predicting cancer drug sensitivity based on the integration of genomic, transcriptomic, and chemical data. Building on prior work that has explored attention-based neural networks, multitask learning, and link prediction approaches, we propose a novel framework that combines the strengths of these methodologies to enhance both the accuracy and interpretability of drug response predictions. Our approach integrates molecular structure information of compounds, gene expression profiles of cancer cells, and biological pathway knowledge through a unified modeling strategy. We demonstrate that incorporating attention mechanisms and leveraging multi-omics data improves the identification of key predictive features, leading to more reliable IC50 predictions. Furthermore, we validate our model using established benchmark datasets and show that it achieves competitive performance compared to existing methods. Our results suggest that integrating diverse data modalities and leveraging network-based representations can significantly improve the predictive power of drug sensitivity models, offering a promising avenue for advancing precision oncology.

original_abstract: The inability to generalize beyond the distribution of a training set is at the core of practical limits of machine learning. We show that the common practice of mixing and shuffling training examples when training deep neural networks is not optimal. On the opposite, partitioning the training data into non-i.i.d. subsets can serve to guide the model to rely on reliable statistical patterns while ignoring spurious correlations in the training data. We demonstrate multiple use cases where these subsets are built using unsupervised clustering, prior knowledge, or other meta-data from existing datasets. The approach is supported by recent results on a causal view of generalization, it is simple to apply, and it demonstrably improves generalization. Applied to the task of visual question answering, we obtain state-of-the-art performance on VQA-CP. We also show improvements over data augmentation using equivalent questions on GQA. Finally, we show a small improvement when training a model simultaneously on VQA v2 and Visual Genome, treating them as two distinct environments rather than one aggregated training set.
generated_abstract: Visual Question Answering (VQA) models have been shown to rely heavily on superficial correlations between questions and answers, often neglecting the visual content of the image. This tendency limits their robustness and real-world applicability. To address this, we propose a novel approach that explicitly encourages models to ground their answers in visual information rather than relying on language priors. Building on prior work that highlights the limitations of current VQA models under varying prior distributions, we introduce a method that disentangles visual concept recognition from answer space identification, ensuring that models do not exploit biases in the training data. Our approach incorporates adversarial regularization to discourage reliance on question-answer co-occurrence patterns, promoting a more balanced integration of visual and linguistic information. We evaluate our method on benchmark datasets designed to test robustness under changing prior distributions and demonstrate significant improvements in performance compared to existing models. Our results confirm that explicitly addressing language priors leads to more reliable and interpretable VQA systems.

original_abstract: Biological evolution has distilled the experiences of many learners into the general learning algorithms of humans. Our novel meta reinforcement learning algorithm MetaGenRL is inspired by this process. MetaGenRL distills the experiences of many complex agents to meta-learn a low-complexity neural objective function that affects how future individuals will learn. Unlike recent meta-RL algorithms, MetaGenRL can generalize to new environments that are entirely different from those used for meta-training. In some cases, it even outperforms human-engineered RL algorithms. MetaGenRL uses off-policy second-order gradients during meta-training that greatly increase its sample efficiency.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of enabling reinforcement learning agents to adapt quickly to new tasks with minimal training data. Building on recent advances in meta-learning and algorithm design, we propose a framework that learns to optimize the learning process itself. Our approach leverages the idea of representing learning algorithms as policies that can be adapted through experience. By training a meta-learner to adjust the parameters of the learning algorithm, we aim to improve the agent's ability to generalize across diverse tasks. We demonstrate that this method allows the agent to achieve high performance on new tasks with only a small number of training samples. Our experiments show that the learned optimization strategy outperforms traditional methods in terms of both speed and robustness. We conclude that learning to optimize the learning process offers a promising direction for developing more efficient and adaptable reinforcement learning systems.

original_abstract: Reed-Muller (RM) codes are among the oldest, simplest and perhaps most ubiquitous family of codes. They are used in many areas of coding theory in both electrical engineering and computer science. Yet, many of their important properties are still under investigation. This paper covers some of the recent developments regarding the weight enumerator and the capacity-achieving properties of RM codes, as well as some of the algorithmic developments. In particular, the paper discusses the recent connections established between RM codes, thresholds of Boolean functions, polarization theory, hypercontractivity, and the techniques of approximating low weight codewords using lower degree polynomials. It then overviews some of the algorithms with performance guarantees, as well as some of the algorithms with state-of-the-art performances in practical regimes. Finally, the paper concludes with a few open problems.
generated_abstract: This paper investigates the capacity-achieving potential of Reed-Muller (RM) codes on binary memoryless symmetric channels by re-examining their relationship with polarization theory. While polar codes achieve capacity through a specific ordering of the generator matrix based on conditional mutual information, RM codes traditionally select rows based on weight. We demonstrate that, when the generator matrix is traversed in the RM code ordering—from the lightest to the heaviest rows—the conditional mutual information also polarizes, albeit at a faster rate than in polar codes. This polarization implies the existence of a distinct code, referred to as the twin-RM code, that is provably capacity-achieving on any binary memoryless symmetric channel. Our results establish a necessary condition for RM codes to achieve capacity and provide a sufficient condition under which the twin-RM code coincides with the RM code itself. We further observe that the twin-RM code and RM code exhibit structural similarities, suggesting they may be equivalent. These findings reconnect RM codes to the theoretical foundation of polarization and offer new insights into their capacity-achieving properties.

original_abstract: To ensure pedestrian friendly streets in the era of automated vehicles, reassessment of current policies, practices, design, rules and regulations of urban areas is of importance. This study investigates pedestrian crossing behaviour, as an important element of urban dynamics that is expected to be affected by the presence of automated vehicles. For this purpose, an interpretable machine learning framework is proposed to explore factors affecting pedestrians' wait time before crossing mid-block crosswalks in the presence of automated vehicles. To collect rich behavioural data, we developed a dynamic and immersive virtual reality experiment, with 180 participants from a heterogeneous population in 4 different locations in the Greater Toronto Area (GTA). Pedestrian wait time behaviour is then analyzed using a data-driven Cox Proportional Hazards (CPH) model, in which the linear combination of the covariates is replaced by a flexible non-linear deep neural network. The proposed model achieved a 5% improvement in goodness of fit, but more importantly, enabled us to incorporate a richer set of covariates. A game theoretic based interpretability method is used to understand the contribution of different covariates to the time pedestrians wait before crossing. Results show that the presence of automated vehicles on roads, wider lane widths, high density on roads, limited sight distance, and lack of walking habits are the main contributing factors to longer wait times. Our study suggested that, to move towards pedestrian-friendly urban areas, national level educational programs for children, enhanced safety measures for seniors, promotion of active modes of transportation, and revised traffic rules and regulations should be considered.
generated_abstract: This paper investigates the complex interactions between pedestrians and autonomous vehicles (AVs) in urban environments, focusing on the decision-making processes that influence pedestrian crossing behavior and trust in AVs. Building on prior work that highlights the importance of non-verbal communication, economic interpretation of behavioral models, and the role of external human-machine interfaces (eHMIs), we propose a framework that integrates behavioral insights with interpretable machine learning models to better understand and predict pedestrian actions. Our approach leverages datasets capturing pedestrian behaviors in mixed traffic conditions and incorporates findings from studies on the impact of eHMIs and traffic signals on pedestrian trust. We develop a model that extracts interpretable economic information from deep neural networks to analyze pedestrian decision-making, including factors such as perceived safety, vehicle behavior, and environmental conditions. Our results demonstrate that pedestrian crossing decisions are influenced by a combination of AV behavior, signal presence, and environmental cues, and that interpretable models can provide valuable insights into these interactions. We conclude that integrating behavioral and machine learning approaches can enhance the design of AV systems that effectively communicate with pedestrians, ultimately improving safety and efficiency in urban traffic environments.

original_abstract: Training neural networks is traditionally done by providing a sequence of random mini-batches sampled uniformly from the entire training data. In this work, we analyze the effect of curriculum learning, which involves the non-uniform sampling of mini-batches, on the training of deep networks, and specifically CNNs trained for image recognition. To employ curriculum learning, the training algorithm must resolve 2 problems: (i) sort the training examples by difficulty; (ii) compute a series of mini-batches that exhibit an increasing level of difficulty. We address challenge (i) using two methods: transfer learning from some competitive ``teacher" network, and bootstrapping. In our empirical evaluation, both methods show similar benefits in terms of increased learning speed and improved final performance on test data. We address challenge (ii) by investigating different pacing functions to guide the sampling. The empirical investigation includes a variety of network architectures, using images from CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and subsets of ImageNet. We conclude with a novel theoretical analysis of curriculum learning, where we show how it effectively modifies the optimization landscape. We then define the concept of an ideal curriculum, and show that under mild conditions it does not change the corresponding global minimum of the optimization function.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of improving the efficiency and effectiveness of training deep neural networks through the development of a novel curriculum learning strategy. Building on prior work that demonstrates the benefits of structured learning paths and dynamic adjustment of training difficulty, we propose a method that automatically generates a curriculum tailored to the learning dynamics of the network. Our approach leverages feedback from the learning process to adaptively select training samples, ensuring that the network is exposed to increasingly complex tasks as it progresses. This method is inspired by the principles of transfer learning and reinforcement learning, where the curriculum is not predefined but instead learned in conjunction with the model. We demonstrate that this adaptive curriculum significantly accelerates convergence and improves generalization performance, particularly in scenarios with noisy or corrupted data. Our experiments show that the proposed approach leads to more robust and efficient training, reducing the need for manual intervention and enabling better performance on challenging tasks.

original_abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks fostered a newfound interest in generative models, resulting in a swelling wave of new works that new-coming researchers may find formidable to surf. In this paper, we intend to help those researchers, by splitting that incoming wave into six "fronts": Architectural Contributions, Conditional Techniques, Normalization and Constraint Contributions, Loss Functions, Image-to-image Translations, and Validation Metrics. The division in fronts organizes literature into approachable blocks, ultimately communicating to the reader how the area is evolving. Previous surveys in the area, which this works also tabulates, focus on a few of those fronts, leaving a gap that we propose to fill with a more integrated, comprehensive overview. Here, instead of an exhaustive survey, we opt for a straightforward review: our target is to be an entry point to this vast literature, and also to be able to update experienced researchers to the newest techniques.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of generating high-resolution, diverse, and realistic images using generative adversarial networks (GANs), while maintaining stable and efficient training. Building on prior work that has introduced architectural innovations, training methodologies, and loss functions to improve image quality, diversity, and training stability, we propose a novel approach that integrates multiple established techniques into a unified framework. Our method incorporates progressive growing strategies to enhance training stability and image quality, employs conditional GANs to enable semantic control over generated outputs, and introduces a style-based generator architecture to achieve fine-grained control over image attributes. We also incorporate mechanisms to increase diversity in generated samples and ensure robust training dynamics. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art results in terms of image quality and diversity across multiple benchmark datasets. We conclude that combining these techniques provides a more effective and reliable foundation for high-resolution image synthesis and manipulation, addressing key limitations of earlier GAN-based methods.

original_abstract: Local differential privacy (LDP) can provide each user with strong privacy guarantees under untrusted data curators while ensuring accurate statistics derived from privatized data. Due to its powerfulness, LDP has been widely adopted to protect privacy in various tasks (e.g., heavy hitters discovery, probability estimation) and systems (e.g., Google Chrome, Apple iOS). Although ${\epsilon}$-LDP has been proposed for many years, the more general notion of $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP has only been studied in very few papers, which mainly consider mean estimation for numeric data. Besides, prior solutions achieve $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP by leveraging Gaussian mechanism, which leads to low accuracy of the aggregated results. In this paper, we propose novel mechanisms that achieve $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP with high utility in data analytics and machine learning. Specifically, we first design $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP algorithms for collecting multi-dimensional numeric data, which can ensure higher accuracy than the optimal Gaussian mechanism while guaranteeing strong privacy for each user. Then, we investigate different local protocols for categorical attributes under $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP. Furthermore, we conduct theoretical analysis on the error bound and variance of the proposed algorithms. Experimental results on real and synthetic datasets demonstrate the high data utility of our proposed algorithms on both simple data statistics and complex machine learning models.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of efficiently collecting and analyzing multidimensional data while ensuring strong local differential privacy (LDP) guarantees. While prior work has made progress in applying LDP to specific data types and tasks, the problem of effectively handling complex, mixed-type data with both numerical and categorical attributes remains underexplored. We build on recent advances in LDP mechanisms for basic statistics and machine learning tasks, extending them to support a broader range of data and analysis scenarios. We propose a novel framework that improves the accuracy of statistical estimation and model training under LDP constraints, particularly for multidimensional data. Our approach ensures that the noise introduced for privacy does not disproportionately affect the quality of the results, enabling more reliable inferences. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods through empirical evaluations on real-world datasets, showing improvements in accuracy over existing LDP solutions. Our results contribute to the development of practical, privacy-preserving data analysis systems that can be deployed in real-world applications.

original_abstract: We investigate the combination of actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithms with uniform large-scale experience replay and propose solutions for two challenges: (a) efficient actor-critic learning with experience replay (b) stability of very off-policy learning. We employ those insights to accelerate hyper-parameter sweeps in which all participating agents run concurrently and share their experience via a common replay module. To this end we analyze the bias-variance tradeoffs in V-trace, a form of importance sampling for actor-critic methods. Based on our analysis, we then argue for mixing experience sampled from replay with on-policy experience, and propose a new trust region scheme that scales effectively to data distributions where V-trace becomes unstable. We provide extensive empirical validation of the proposed solution. We further show the benefits of this setup by demonstrating state-of-the-art data efficiency on Atari among agents trained up until 200M environment frames.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of improving the efficiency and effectiveness of deep reinforcement learning in complex, high-dimensional environments. Building on prior work that has demonstrated the potential of distributed architectures, prioritized experience replay, and off-policy learning, we propose a novel framework that integrates these advancements into a unified approach. Our method combines distributed training with prioritized experience replay and off-policy corrections to enhance learning stability and data efficiency. We introduce a modular architecture that allows for flexible integration of different algorithmic components, enabling the system to adapt to a wide range of tasks. By leveraging the strengths of existing techniques, our approach achieves significant improvements in training speed and final performance across multiple benchmark domains. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of both sample efficiency and asymptotic performance, while maintaining stability across diverse environments. These results suggest that the integration of distributed training, prioritized experience replay, and off-policy learning can lead to substantial improvements in deep reinforcement learning.

original_abstract: The design of deep graph models still remains to be investigated and the crucial part is how to explore and exploit the knowledge from different hops of neighbors in an efficient way. In this paper, we propose a novel RNN-like deep graph neural network architecture by incorporating AdaBoost into the computation of network; and the proposed graph convolutional network called AdaGCN~(AdaBoosting Graph Convolutional Network) has the ability to efficiently extract knowledge from high-order neighbors and integrate knowledge from different hops of neighbors into the network in an AdaBoost way. We also present the architectural difference between AdaGCN and existing graph convolutional methods to show the benefits of our proposal. Finally, extensive experiments demonstrate the state-of-the-art prediction performance and the computational advantage of our approach AdaGCN.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of effectively learning node representations on graph-structured data while maintaining scalability and interpretability. Building on prior work that generalizes convolutional neural networks to graphs, we focus on the limitations of existing methods in capturing multi-scale neighborhood relationships and their impact on model performance. We propose a novel architecture that enhances the ability of graph neural networks to learn from diverse neighborhood ranges by incorporating a flexible mechanism for aggregating information across different scales. This approach allows the model to adaptively combine representations derived from varying distances in the graph, improving its capacity to capture both local and global structural patterns. Our method is designed to maintain linear computational complexity and compatibility with semi-supervised learning settings. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive performance while offering greater flexibility and interpretability compared to existing methods. The results highlight the importance of considering multi-scale information in graph representation learning and suggest that adaptive aggregation strategies can lead to more robust and effective models.

original_abstract: This paper seeks to answer a simple but fundamental question: what role can non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) play in massive multi-in multi-out (MIMO)? It is well established that power-domain NOMA schemes can outperform conventional orthogonal multiple access schemes in cellular networks. However, this fact does not imply that NOMA is the most efficient way to communicate in massive MIMO setups, where the base stations have many more antennas than there are users in the cell. These setups are becoming the norm in future networks and are usually studied by assuming spatial multiplexing of the users using linear multi-user beamforming. To answer the above-mentioned question, we analyze and compare the performance achieved by NOMA and multi-user beamforming in both non-line-of-sight and line-of-sight scenarios. We reveal that the latter scheme gives the highest average sum rate in massive MIMO setups. We also identify specific cases where NOMA is the better choice in massive MIMO and explain how NOMA plays an essential role in creating a hybrid of NOMA and multi-user beamforming that is shown to perform better than two standalone schemes do.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of achieving efficient and reliable communication in dense wireless networks by combining the benefits of massive MIMO and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA). Building on prior work that highlights the potential of massive MIMO to improve throughput and energy efficiency, and the advantages of NOMA in supporting multiple users within the same resource block, we propose a novel framework that integrates these two technologies. Our approach focuses on optimizing power allocation and beamforming strategies to enhance system performance while addressing the limitations of existing methods in terms of feedback overhead and channel estimation accuracy. We derive analytical expressions for achievable rates under different channel conditions and propose a low-complexity optimization scheme that balances performance and computational demands. Our results demonstrate that the proposed framework can achieve significant gains in spectral efficiency and user fairness compared to conventional orthogonal multiple access schemes, particularly in scenarios with limited feedback and imperfect channel state information. The study concludes that the integration of massive MIMO and NOMA offers a promising direction for future high-capacity wireless networks, provided that the challenges related to channel estimation and interference management are effectively addressed.

original_abstract: In [1, 2], we have explored the theoretical aspects of feature extraction optimization processes for solving largescale problems and overcoming machine learning limitations. Majority of optimization algorithms that have been introduced in [1, 2] guarantee the optimal performance of supervised learning, given offline and discrete data, to deal with curse of dimensionality (CoD) problem. These algorithms, however, are not tailored for solving emerging learning problems. One of the important issues caused by online data is lack of sufficient samples per class. Further, traditional machine learning algorithms cannot achieve accurate training based on limited distributed data, as data has proliferated and dispersed significantly. Machine learning employs a strict model or embedded engine to train and predict which still fails to learn unseen classes and sufficiently use online data. In this chapter, we introduce these challenges elaborately. We further investigate Meta-Learning (MTL) algorithm, and their application and promises to solve the emerging problems by answering how autonomous agents can learn to learn?.
generated_abstract: Few-shot learning remains a critical challenge in machine learning, particularly in scenarios where only a limited number of examples are available for new classes. While prior work has introduced various approaches, including metric learning, relation networks, and meta-learning, these methods often struggle with task ambiguity, computational efficiency, or generalization across diverse task structures. This paper addresses these limitations by proposing a novel framework that integrates meta-learning with probabilistic modeling to enhance robustness and adaptability in few-shot settings. Building on existing methods such as model-agnostic meta-learning and hierarchical meta-learning, we introduce a probabilistic extension that enables the sampling of multiple plausible models for a new task, thereby improving performance in ambiguous conditions. Our approach incorporates a variational lower bound to train a parameter distribution, allowing for stochastic adaptation during inference. This method not only improves generalization but also maintains computational efficiency. Experiments on standard few-shot benchmarks demonstrate that our framework achieves competitive performance while offering greater flexibility in handling heterogeneous tasks.

original_abstract: Edge computing is an emerging concept based on distributing computing, storage, and control services closer to end network nodes. Edge computing lies at the heart of the fifth generation (5G) wireless systems and beyond. While current state-of-the-art networks communicate, compute, and process data in a centralized manner (at the cloud), for latency and compute-centric applications, both radio access and computational resources must be brought closer to the edge, harnessing the availability of computing and storage-enabled small cell base stations in proximity to the end devices. Furthermore, the network infrastructure must enable a distributed edge decision-making service that learns to adapt to the network dynamics with minimal latency and optimize network deployment and operation accordingly. This article will provide a fresh look to the concept of edge computing by first discussing the applications that the network edge must provide, with a special emphasis on the ensuing challenges in enabling ultra-reliable and low-latency edge computing services for mission-critical applications such as virtual reality (VR), vehicle-to-everything (V2X), edge artificial intelligence (AI), and so forth. Furthermore, several case studies where the edge is key are explored followed by insights and prospect for future work.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of achieving energy-efficient and reliable task execution in mobile edge computing (MEC) environments, where both latency and reliability constraints are critical. Building on prior work that explores user-centric mobility management, latency-aware task offloading, and edge intelligence, we focus on the joint optimization of resource allocation, task offloading, and user-server association under dynamic wireless conditions. Our approach integrates probabilistic constraints on task queues and leverages tools from extreme value theory and Lyapunov optimization to ensure robust performance in the face of temporal and spatial variability. We propose a two-timescale mechanism that dynamically adjusts user-server associations and resource allocations to meet stringent reliability and latency requirements while minimizing energy consumption. The proposed framework is designed to operate effectively in ultra-dense and heterogeneous network environments, where traditional average-based metrics are insufficient. Our results demonstrate that the approach achieves significant improvements in reliability and latency compared to conventional methods, while maintaining energy efficiency. This work contributes to the ongoing effort to realize intelligent, low-latency, and reliable edge computing systems that support mission-critical applications.

original_abstract: Automatic Post-Editing (APE) aims to correct systematic errors in a machine translated text. This is primarily useful when the machine translation (MT) system is not accessible for improvement, leaving APE as a viable option to improve translation quality as a downstream task - which is the focus of this thesis. This field has received less attention compared to MT due to several reasons, which include: the limited availability of data to perform a sound research, contrasting views reported by different researchers about the effectiveness of APE, and limited attention from the industry to use APE in current production pipelines. In this thesis, we perform a thorough investigation of APE as a downstream task in order to: i) understand its potential to improve translation quality; ii) advance the core technology - starting from classical methods to recent deep-learning based solutions; iii) cope with limited and sparse data; iv) better leverage multiple input sources; v) mitigate the task-specific problem of over-correction; vi) enhance neural decoding to leverage external knowledge; and vii) establish an online learning framework to handle data diversity in real-time. All the above contributions are discussed across several chapters, and most of them are evaluated in the APE shared task organized each year at the Conference on Machine Translation. Our efforts in improving the technology resulted in the best system at the 2017 APE shared task, and our work on online learning received a distinguished paper award at the Italian Conference on Computational Linguistics. Overall, outcomes and findings of our work have boost interest among researchers and attracted industries to examine this technology to solve real-word problems.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of improving the quality of machine translation outputs through automatic post-editing (APE), focusing on the integration of neural machine translation (NMT) models with quality estimation (QE) techniques. Building on recent advances in NMT and APE, we explore the potential of combining neural models with QE features to guide the post-editing process more effectively. We propose a framework that leverages the outputs of multiple NMT models, enriched with QE features, to generate more accurate and fluent post-edited translations. By incorporating QE signals into the APE process, we aim to better align the post-editing decisions with the actual quality of the initial translation. Our approach is evaluated on standard APE benchmarks, demonstrating improvements in both automatic and human evaluation metrics. The results indicate that integrating QE features into the APE system enhances the ability to identify and correct errors while preserving the fluency and coherence of the translation. This work contributes to the ongoing effort to bridge the gap between translation quality estimation and post-editing, offering a more informed and effective approach to refining machine translation outputs.

original_abstract: We consider a variant of the classic Ski Rental online algorithm with applications to machine learning. In our variant, we allow the skier access to a black-box machine-learning algorithm that provides an estimate of the probability that there will be at most a threshold number of ski-days. We derive a class of optimal randomized algorithms to determine the strategy that minimizes the worst-case expected competitive ratio for the skier given a prediction from the machine learning algorithm,and analyze the performance and robustness of these algorithms.
generated_abstract: In this paper, we address the challenge of leveraging machine-learned predictions to improve the performance of online decision-making systems, while ensuring robustness against prediction errors. Building on prior work that demonstrates how to integrate learned advice into online algorithms, we focus on developing strategies that adaptively use predictions to achieve performance guarantees that depend on the quality of the input. We propose a general framework for modifying classical online algorithms to incorporate predictions in a way that maintains strong worst-case bounds while achieving significant improvements when the predictions are accurate. Our approach ensures that the performance of the algorithm degrades gracefully as the prediction error increases. We analyze the theoretical properties of this framework and demonstrate its applicability to a range of problems, showing that it can lead to better average-case performance without sacrificing worst-case guarantees. Our results highlight the potential of combining machine learning with online algorithms to achieve practical improvements in real-world settings.

original_abstract: While deep learning (DL)-based networked systems have shown great potential in various applications, a key drawback is that Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) in DL are blackboxes and nontransparent for network operators. The lack of interpretability makes DL-based networked systems challenging to operate and troubleshoot, which further prevents DL-based networked systems from deploying in practice. In this paper, we propose TranSys, a novel framework to explain DL-based networked systems for practical deployment. Transys categorizes current DL-based networked systems and introduces different explanation methods based on decision tree and hypergraph to effectively explain DL-based networked systems. TranSys can explain the DNN policies in the form of decision trees and highlight critical components based on analysis over hypergraph. We evaluate TranSys over several typical DL-based networked systems and demonstrate that Transys can provide human-readable explanations for network operators. We also present three use cases of Transys, which could (i) help network operators troubleshoot DL-based networked systems, (ii) improve the decision latency and resource consumption of DL-based networked systems by ~10x on different metrics, and (iii) provide suggestions on daily operations for network operators when incidences occur.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of interpreting and verifying complex machine learning models deployed in critical networking systems, where the opacity of decision-making processes can hinder trust and reliability. Building on prior work that explores interpretability techniques for deep learning models and graph neural networks, as well as methods for verifying deep reinforcement learning systems, we propose a unified approach to evaluate and explain the behavior of machine learning models in networking contexts. Our approach integrates post hoc explanation techniques with formal verification methods to provide both human-understandable insights into model decisions and guarantees about their adherence to specified constraints. We apply this framework to analyze models used in packet classification, network optimization, and resource management, demonstrating how interpretability and verification can be combined to enhance the safety and performance of machine learning-driven systems. Our results highlight the importance of interpretability in identifying unexpected behaviors and the value of formal verification in ensuring compliance with system requirements. We conclude that combining these approaches offers a promising path toward more trustworthy and reliable machine learning systems in networking applications.

original_abstract: This paper proposes the first model-free Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework to synthesise policies for unknown, and continuous-state Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), such that a given linear temporal property is satisfied. We convert the given property into a Limit Deterministic Buchi Automaton (LDBA), namely a finite-state machine expressing the property. Exploiting the structure of the LDBA, we shape a synchronous reward function on-the-fly, so that an RL algorithm can synthesise a policy resulting in traces that probabilistically satisfy the linear temporal property. This probability (certificate) is also calculated in parallel with policy learning when the state space of the MDP is finite: as such, the RL algorithm produces a policy that is certified with respect to the property. Under the assumption of finite state space, theoretical guarantees are provided on the convergence of the RL algorithm to an optimal policy, maximising the above probability. We also show that our method produces ''best available'' control policies when the logical property cannot be satisfied. In the general case of a continuous state space, we propose a neural network architecture for RL and we empirically show that the algorithm finds satisfying policies, if there exist such policies. The performance of the proposed framework is evaluated via a set of numerical examples and benchmarks, where we observe an improvement of one order of magnitude in the number of iterations required for the policy synthesis, compared to existing approaches whenever available.
generated_abstract: We address the challenge of synthesizing control policies for unknown Markov decision processes (MDPs) that maximize an a priori unknown performance criterion while ensuring satisfaction of temporal logic specifications. Building on prior work that integrates temporal logic constraints with reinforcement learning (RL), we propose a method that decouples the problem into two stages: first, deriving a permissive strategy that ensures compliance with the specification, and second, optimizing within this strategy using a reward function that captures the unknown performance metric. Our approach leverages maximin-Q learning to achieve both correctness with respect to the temporal logic constraints and optimality with respect to the performance criterion. We establish theoretical guarantees for correctness and demonstrate that the method is applicable to a broad class of temporal logic specifications, with sub-optimality possible for more complex cases. We present an algorithm that realizes this approach and evaluate its computational requirements and effectiveness through illustrative examples.

original_abstract: Many inferential and learning tasks can be accomplished efficiently by means of distributed optimization algorithms where the network topology plays a critical role in driving the local interactions among neighboring agents. There is a large body of literature examining the effect of the graph structure on the performance of optimization strategies. In this article, we examine the inverse problem and consider the reverse question: How much information does observing the behavior at the nodes convey about the underlying network structure used for optimization? Over large-scale networks, the difficulty of addressing such inverse questions (or problems) is compounded by the fact that usually only a limited portion of nodes can be probed, giving rise to a second important question: Despite the presence of several unobserved nodes, are partial and local observations still sufficient to discover the graph linking the probed nodes? The article surveys recent advances on this inverse learning problem and related questions. Examples of applications are provided to illustrate how the interplay between graph learning and distributed optimization arises in practice, e.g., in cognitive engineered systems such as distributed detection, or in other real-world problems such as the mechanism of opinion formation over social networks and the mechanism of coordination in biological networks. A unifying framework for examining the reconstruction error will be described, which allows to devise and examine various estimation strategies enabling successful graph learning. The relevance of specific network attributes, such as sparsity versus density of connections, and node degree concentration, is discussed in relation to the topology inference goal. It is shown how universal (i.e., data-driven) clustering algorithms can be exploited to solve the graph learning problem.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of inferring the topology of a network from observations of signals or outputs that have been diffused across its nodes, in scenarios where the underlying graph structure is unknown. Building on prior work that explores the relationship between graph structure and signal diffusion, we focus on characterizing the set of graphs that are consistent with observed stationary signals, particularly those that have undergone diffusion from an initial i.i.d. state. We establish that this set of valid graphs is closely tied to the eigenvectors of the signal covariance matrix and forms a convex set. We further explore the implications of this characterization for graph recovery, proposing methods to select specific graphs within this set based on criteria such as simplicity and sparsity. Additionally, we introduce a metric to assess how well a graph aligns with the stationarity assumption. Our approach is validated through experiments on real-world data, demonstrating its relevance to existing methods in the field. The results highlight the importance of considering the spectral properties of signals in the context of network inference.

original_abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has recently led to many breakthroughs on a range of complex control tasks. However, the agent's decision-making process is generally not transparent. The lack of interpretability hinders the applicability of RL in safety-critical scenarios. While several methods have attempted to interpret vision-based RL, most come without detailed explanation for the agent's behaviour. In this paper, we propose a self-supervised interpretable framework, which can discover causal features to enable easy interpretation of RL agents even for non-experts. Specifically, a self-supervised interpretable network (SSINet) is employed to produce fine-grained attention masks for highlighting task-relevant information, which constitutes most evidence for the agent's decisions. We verify and evaluate our method on several Atari 2600 games as well as Duckietown, which is a challenging self-driving car simulator environment. The results show that our method renders causal explanations and empirical evidences about how the agent makes decisions and why the agent performs well or badly, especially when transferred to novel scenes. Overall, our method provides valuable insight into the internal decision-making process of vision-based RL. In addition, our method does not use any external labelled data, and thus demonstrates the possibility to learn high-quality mask through a self-supervised manner, which may shed light on new paradigms for label-free vision learning such as self-supervised segmentation and detection.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of interpreting deep reinforcement learning agents by examining their visual attention patterns during decision making. Building on prior work that integrates attention mechanisms into reinforcement learning and develops methods for visualizing agent behavior, we propose a novel framework that enhances both the interpretability and performance of deep Q-networks. Our approach incorporates attention-based saliency generation directly into the learning process, enabling the agent to focus on task-relevant regions of the input while maintaining competitive performance on Atari 2600 games. By analyzing the attention maps produced during training and evaluation, we provide insights into the strategies agents use to achieve high rewards. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method not only improves the transparency of deep reinforcement learning models but also supports a better understanding of how agents evolve during learning. We conclude that integrating attention mechanisms into the learning process offers a promising path toward more interpretable and effective reinforcement learning systems.

original_abstract: Concolic testing is a test generation technique which works effectively by integrating random testing generation and symbolic execution. Existing concolic testing engines focus on numeric programs. Heap-manipulating programs make extensive use of complex heap objects like trees and lists. Testing such programs is challenging due to multiple reasons. Firstly, test inputs for such program are required to satisfy non-trivial constraints which must be specified precisely. Secondly, precisely encoding and solving path conditions in such programs are challenging and often expensive. In this work, we propose the first concolic testing engine called CSF for heap-manipulating programs based on separation logic. CSF effectively combines specification-based testing and concolic execution for test input generation. It is evaluated on a set of challenging heap-manipulating programs. The results show that CSF generates valid test inputs with high coverage efficiently. Furthermore, we show that CSF can be potentially used in combination with precondition inference tools to reduce the user effort.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of effectively testing and verifying JavaScript programs with complex heap structures, where existing symbolic execution techniques struggle to generate valid and meaningful test inputs. Building on recent advances in compositional symbolic execution and separation logic, we propose a novel approach that integrates whole-program symbolic testing with automatic compositional reasoning to improve the precision and scalability of test input generation. Our method leverages bi-abduction to infer resource constraints and guide the symbolic execution process, ensuring that generated test inputs are fully initialized and structurally valid. By combining the strengths of symbolic execution and compositional reasoning, we aim to overcome the limitations of existing tools in handling unbounded heap structures and complex data dependencies. Our evaluation on a set of JavaScript data-structure libraries demonstrates the feasibility of this approach, showing improvements in test coverage and reduction in invalid test inputs. The results suggest that integrating compositional reasoning into symbolic execution can significantly enhance the effectiveness of automated testing for programs with complex heap manipulations.

original_abstract: Prior work on controllable text generation usually assumes that the controlled attribute can take on one of a small set of values known a priori. In this work, we propose a novel task, where the syntax of a generated sentence is controlled rather by a sentential exemplar. To evaluate quantitatively with standard metrics, we create a novel dataset with human annotations. We also develop a variational model with a neural module specifically designed for capturing syntactic knowledge and several multitask training objectives to promote disentangled representation learning. Empirically, the proposed model is observed to achieve improvements over baselines and learn to capture desirable characteristics.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of generating natural language text with explicit control over high-level semantic and syntactic properties. Building on recent advances in variational autoencoders and latent representation learning, we propose a generative model that leverages distributed latent representations of entire sentences to enable controlled text generation. Our approach incorporates techniques for disentangling sentence-level attributes and utilizes latent edit vectors to guide the generation process. By combining methods for modeling holistic sentence properties with strategies for improving language modeling performance, we aim to produce diverse, coherent, and semantically meaningful outputs. We demonstrate that our model can generate sentences with desired attributes through structured manipulation of the latent space, while maintaining fluency and grammatical correctness. Our experiments show that the proposed method achieves improvements in both quality and controllability compared to baseline approaches, and we explore the interpretability of the learned representations. The results suggest that explicit modeling of sentence-level properties can lead to more effective and flexible text generation systems.

original_abstract: Hyperspectral images (HSI) provide rich spectral information that contributed to the successful performance improvement of numerous computer vision tasks. However, it can only be achieved at the expense of images' spatial resolution. Hyperspectral image super-resolution (HSI-SR) addresses this problem by fusing low resolution (LR) HSI with multispectral image (MSI) carrying much higher spatial resolution (HR). All existing HSI-SR approaches require the LR HSI and HR MSI to be well registered and the reconstruction accuracy of the HR HSI relies heavily on the registration accuracy of different modalities. This paper exploits the uncharted problem domain of HSI-SR without the requirement of multi-modality registration. Given the unregistered LR HSI and HR MSI with overlapped regions, we design a unique unsupervised learning structure linking the two unregistered modalities by projecting them into the same statistical space through the same encoder. The mutual information (MI) is further adopted to capture the non-linear statistical dependencies between the representations from two modalities (carrying spatial information) and their raw inputs. By maximizing the MI, spatial correlations between different modalities can be well characterized to further reduce the spectral distortion. A collaborative $l_{2,1}$ norm is employed as the reconstruction error instead of the more common $l_2$ norm, so that individual pixels can be recovered as accurately as possible. With this design, the network allows to extract correlated spectral and spatial information from unregistered images that better preserves the spectral information. The proposed method is referred to as unregistered and unsupervised mutual Dirichlet Net ($u^2$-MDN). Extensive experimental results using benchmark HSI datasets demonstrate the superior performance of $u^2$-MDN as compared to the state-of-the-art.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of enhancing the spatial resolution of hyperspectral images while preserving their rich spectral information. Building on recent advances in deep learning for image super-resolution and fusion, we propose a novel framework that integrates spatial constraints with a deep spectral difference convolutional neural network (SDCNN) to achieve high-quality hyperspectral image super-resolution. Our approach ensures that the reconstructed high-resolution hyperspectral image remains spectrally consistent with the input low-resolution data. By incorporating a spatial constraint strategy, we maintain spatial fidelity during the super-resolution process, while the SDCNN model learns the end-to-end mapping between low- and high-resolution hyperspectral images. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of spatial enhancement and spectral preservation, offering a robust and effective solution for hyperspectral image super-resolution.

original_abstract: This paper presents SimCLR: a simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations. We simplify recently proposed contrastive self-supervised learning algorithms without requiring specialized architectures or a memory bank. In order to understand what enables the contrastive prediction tasks to learn useful representations, we systematically study the major components of our framework. We show that (1) composition of data augmentations plays a critical role in defining effective predictive tasks, (2) introducing a learnable nonlinear transformation between the representation and the contrastive loss substantially improves the quality of the learned representations, and (3) contrastive learning benefits from larger batch sizes and more training steps compared to supervised learning. By combining these findings, we are able to considerably outperform previous methods for self-supervised and semi-supervised learning on ImageNet. A linear classifier trained on self-supervised representations learned by SimCLR achieves 76.5% top-1 accuracy, which is a 7% relative improvement over previous state-of-the-art, matching the performance of a supervised ResNet-50. When fine-tuned on only 1% of the labels, we achieve 85.8% top-5 accuracy, outperforming AlexNet with 100X fewer labels.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of learning high-level visual representations without relying on extensive manual annotations. Building on recent advances in unsupervised and self-supervised learning, we explore methods that leverage intrinsic properties of visual data to train deep convolutional networks. Our approach focuses on designing pretext tasks that encourage the model to learn discriminative and semantically meaningful features. By maximizing mutual information across different views of the same image or context, we aim to capture high-level factors that are consistent across transformations. We evaluate our method on standard benchmarks for unsupervised learning, including ImageNet classification and PASCAL VOC object detection. Our results demonstrate that the learned representations achieve strong performance, significantly narrowing the gap between unsupervised and supervised learning. We show that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches in several transfer learning scenarios, highlighting the potential of self-supervised learning for visual representation learning. Our findings suggest that carefully designed pretext tasks can enable models to learn rich visual features without explicit supervision.

original_abstract: Existing analysis work in machine reading comprehension (MRC) is largely concerned with evaluating the capabilities of systems. However, the capabilities of datasets are not assessed for benchmarking language understanding precisely. We propose a semi-automated, ablation-based methodology for this challenge; By checking whether questions can be solved even after removing features associated with a skill requisite for language understanding, we evaluate to what degree the questions do not require the skill. Experiments on 10 datasets (e.g., CoQA, SQuAD v2.0, and RACE) with a strong baseline model show that, for example, the relative scores of a baseline model provided with content words only and with shuffled sentence words in the context are on average 89.2% and 78.5% of the original score, respectively. These results suggest that most of the questions already answered correctly by the model do not necessarily require grammatical and complex reasoning. For precise benchmarking, MRC datasets will need to take extra care in their design to ensure that questions can correctly evaluate the intended skills.
generated_abstract: We address the challenge of evaluating machine reading comprehension systems on tasks that require deeper language understanding and multi-sentence reasoning. While existing datasets have driven progress in answering questions based on single passages, they often fail to capture the complexity of real-world comprehension, which involves integrating information across multiple sentences and contexts. Building on recent efforts such as SQuAD, DuoRC, and the AI2 Reasoning Challenge, we introduce a new benchmark that emphasizes multi-sentence inference and reasoning over diverse textual domains. Our dataset is constructed through a rigorous crowdsourcing process, ensuring that questions require integration of information from multiple parts of a passage. We analyze baseline models and find that even state-of-the-art systems struggle with this task, achieving significantly lower performance compared to human levels. This highlights the need for models that can better capture the nuances of language and reasoning across extended contexts. Our work provides a new challenge for the community to develop systems capable of more robust and comprehensive reading comprehension.

original_abstract: Spatio-temporal action localization is a challenging yet fascinating task that aims to detect and classify human actions in video clips. In this paper, we develop a high-level video understanding module which can encode interactions between actors and objects both in space and time. In our formulation, spatio-temporal relationships are learned by performing self-attention operations on a graph structure connecting entities from consecutive clips. Noticeably, the use of graph learning is unprecedented for this task. From a computational point of view, the proposed module is backbone independent by design and does not need end-to-end training. When tested on the AVA dataset, it demonstrates a 10-16% relative mAP improvement over the baseline. Further, it can outperform or bring performances comparable to state-of-the-art models which require heavy end-to-end and synchronized training on multiple GPUs. Code is publicly available at: this https URL.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of effectively modeling spatiotemporal dynamics in video for action recognition. While prior work has explored various approaches, including 3D convolutions, two-stream networks, and residual learning, the integration of spatial and temporal information remains a critical challenge. We propose a novel architecture that builds on the principles of spatiotemporal residual learning and collaborative feature fusion. Our approach introduces a unified framework that enhances the interaction between spatial and temporal streams through structured residual connections and parameter sharing. This enables more effective learning of complementary features while maintaining computational efficiency. We demonstrate that our method achieves strong performance on standard benchmarks, showing improvements in both accuracy and interpretability. Our results suggest that structured integration of spatial and temporal information can lead to more robust and generalizable models for video action recognition.

original_abstract: Low bit-width integer weights and activations are very important for efficient inference, especially with respect to lower power consumption. We propose Monte Carlo methods to quantize the weights and activations of pre-trained neural networks without any re-training. By performing importance sampling we obtain quantized low bit-width integer values from full-precision weights and activations. The precision, sparsity, and complexity are easily configurable by the amount of sampling performed. Our approach, called Monte Carlo Quantization (MCQ), is linear in both time and space, with the resulting quantized, sparse networks showing minimal accuracy loss when compared to the original full-precision networks. Our method either outperforms or achieves competitive results on multiple benchmarks compared to previous quantization methods that do require additional training.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of training deep neural networks with low-precision weights and activations while maintaining high prediction accuracy. Building on prior work that demonstrates the feasibility of using binary, ternary, and low-bitwidth representations for both training and inference, we propose a method that integrates learned quantization with the training process to minimize accuracy degradation. Our approach jointly optimizes the network and its quantizers, allowing for flexible precision levels across weights and activations. By training the quantization parameters alongside the network, we achieve a better alignment between the quantized and full-precision models, resulting in improved performance compared to fixed quantization schemes. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that our method achieves competitive accuracy with full-precision models while significantly reducing model size and computational requirements. We conclude that learned quantization provides a promising path toward deploying efficient, compact deep neural networks on resource-constrained hardware without sacrificing performance.

original_abstract: The advent of deep learning has given rise to neural scene representations - learned mathematical models of a 3D environment. However, many of these representations do not explicitly reason about geometry and thus do not account for the underlying 3D structure of the scene. In contrast, geometric deep learning has explored 3D-structure-aware representations of scene geometry, but requires explicit 3D supervision. We propose Scene Representation Networks (SRNs), a continuous, 3D-structure-aware scene representation that encodes both geometry and appearance. SRNs represent scenes as continuous functions that map world coordinates to a feature representation of local scene properties. By formulating the image formation as a differentiable ray-marching algorithm, SRNs can be trained end-to-end from only 2D observations, without access to depth or geometry. This formulation naturally generalizes across scenes, learning powerful geometry and appearance priors in the process. We demonstrate the potential of SRNs by evaluating them for novel view synthesis, few-shot reconstruction, joint shape and appearance interpolation, and unsupervised discovery of a non-rigid face model.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of reconstructing 3D object representations from single 2D images without explicit 3D supervision or annotations. Building on recent advances in learning implicit 3D representations and view synthesis, we propose a novel framework that leverages persistent 3D feature embeddings to infer the underlying geometry and appearance of objects. Our approach combines insights from view-dependent appearance modeling with unsupervised learning strategies that enable the system to generate multi-view images and depth maps from a single input. By learning to disentangle 3D structure from viewpoint and texture, the model can synthesize novel views and reconstruct 3D shapes without requiring labeled 3D data or multiple input views. We demonstrate that our method achieves competitive performance on single-view 3D reconstruction tasks, showing robustness to variations in object class, viewpoint, and background. Our results indicate that the proposed approach advances the ability to learn 3D representations from natural images in an unsupervised manner, opening new possibilities for applications in computer vision and graphics.

original_abstract: AI Ethics is now a global topic of discussion in academic and policy circles. At least 84 public-private initiatives have produced statements describing high-level principles, values, and other tenets to guide the ethical development, deployment, and governance of AI. According to recent meta-analyses, AI Ethics has seemingly converged on a set of principles that closely resemble the four classic principles of medical ethics. Despite the initial credibility granted to a principled approach to AI Ethics by the connection to principles in medical ethics, there are reasons to be concerned about its future impact on AI development and governance. Significant differences exist between medicine and AI development that suggest a principled approach in the latter may not enjoy success comparable to the former. Compared to medicine, AI development lacks (1) common aims and fiduciary duties, (2) professional history and norms, (3) proven methods to translate principles into practice, and (4) robust legal and professional accountability mechanisms. These differences suggest we should not yet celebrate consensus around high-level principles that hide deep political and normative disagreement.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of aligning ethical principles with practical implementation in machine learning systems, focusing on the gap between theoretical guidelines and real-world application. Building on prior work that highlights the need for actionable tools and the ethical concerns raised by algorithmic decision-making, we explore how industry practitioners navigate fairness, transparency, and accountability in their workflows. We propose a structured approach to integrate ethical considerations into the development lifecycle, informed by the identified needs and challenges of practitioners. Our approach emphasizes the translation of abstract ethical principles into concrete, implementable practices, leveraging insights from existing literature on fairness, opacity, and ethical frameworks. We conclude that while existing guidelines provide a foundation, their effective application requires tailored methods that address the specific constraints and priorities of industry teams. This work contributes to the ongoing effort to bridge the divide between ethical aspirations and practical realities in AI development.

original_abstract: This paper develops several average-case reduction techniques to show new hardness results for three central high-dimensional statistics problems, implying a statistical-computational gap induced by robustness, a detection-recovery gap and a universality principle for these gaps. A main feature of our approach is to map to these problems via a common intermediate problem that we introduce, which we call Imbalanced Sparse Gaussian Mixtures. We assume the planted clique conjecture for a version of the planted clique problem where the position of the planted clique is mildly constrained, and from this obtain the following computational lower bounds: (1) a $k$-to-$k^2$ statistical-computational gap for robust sparse mean estimation, providing the first average-case evidence for a conjecture of Li (2017) and Balakrishnan et al.
