(2017); (2) a tight lower bound for semirandom planted dense subgraph, which shows that a semirandom adversary shifts the detection threshold in planted dense subgraph to the conjectured recovery threshold; and (3) a universality principle for $k$-to-$k^2$ gaps in a broad class of sparse mixture problems that includes many natural formulations such as the spiked covariance model. #R##N#Our main approach is to introduce several average-case techniques to produce structured and Gaussianized versions of an input graph problem, and then to rotate these high-dimensional Gaussians by matrices carefully constructed from hyperplanes in $\mathbb{F}_r^t$. For our universality result, we introduce a new method to perform an algorithmic change of measure tailored to sparse mixtures. We also provide evidence that the mild promise in our variant of planted clique does not change the complexity of the problem.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of understanding the interplay between statistical and computational feasibility in high-dimensional inference problems involving planted sparse structures. Building on prior work that has identified statistical-computational gaps in problems such as sparse PCA, planted clique, and submatrix localization, we aim to characterize the fundamental limits of detection and recovery in these settings. We propose a unified framework that leverages average-case reductions from conjecturally hard problems to establish tight computational lower bounds for a broad class of planted sparse structure detection tasks. Our approach relies on the planted clique conjecture and extends it to various models, including sparse PCA, submatrix localization, and variants of the stochastic block model. We show that for certain sparsity levels, no polynomial-time algorithm can achieve optimal detection, thereby revealing a sharp computational barrier. Our results confirm that the statistical limits of these problems can be fundamentally distinct from their computational counterparts, and they highlight the importance of considering both aspects when designing and analyzing algorithms for high-dimensional inference. We conclude that the existence of these gaps suggests that achieving statistical optimality may require algorithms that are not computationally efficient, and that understanding these tradeoffs is essential for advancing the field of high-dimensional statistics.

original_abstract: The desire to map neural networks to varying-capacity devices has led to the development of a wealth of compression techniques, many of which involve replacing standard convolutional blocks in a large network with cheap alternative blocks. However, not all blocks are created equally; for a required compute budget there may exist a potent combination of many different cheap blocks, though exhaustively searching for such a combination is prohibitively expensive. In this work, we develop BlockSwap: a fast algorithm for choosing networks with interleaved block types by passing a single minibatch of training data through randomly initialised networks and gauging their Fisher potential. These networks can then be used as students and distilled with the original large network as a teacher. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the chosen networks across CIFAR-10 and ImageNet for classification, and COCO for detection, and provide a comprehensive ablation study of our approach. BlockSwap quickly explores possible block configurations using a simple architecture ranking system, yielding highly competitive networks in orders of magnitude less time than most architecture search techniques (e.g. under 5 minutes on a single GPU for CIFAR-10). Code is available at https://github.com/BayesWatch/pytorch-blockswap.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of reducing the computational and memory demands of deep neural networks while maintaining their accuracy and performance. Building on prior work that explores parameter pruning, network compression, and efficient architectures, we propose a novel approach that integrates multiple strategies for achieving compact and efficient models. Our method systematically identifies and removes redundant parameters and connections, leveraging insights from neuron-level pruning, hierarchical filter grouping, and learned group convolutions. By combining these techniques, we aim to reduce the number of parameters and operations without sacrificing model accuracy. We validate our approach on standard benchmark datasets, demonstrating significant reductions in model size and computational cost while maintaining or improving performance over existing methods. Our results indicate that the proposed approach is broadly applicable across different network architectures and tasks, offering a practical solution for deploying deep learning models on resource-constrained platforms.

original_abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of generating a set ofrealistic and diverse backgrounds when given only a smallforeground region. We refer to this task as image outpaint-ing. The technical challenge of this task is to synthesize notonly plausible but also diverse image outputs. Traditionalgenerative adversarial networks suffer from mode collapse.While recent approaches propose to maximize orpreserve the pairwise distance between generated sampleswith respect to their latent distance, they do not explicitlyprevent the diverse samples of different conditional inputsfrom collapsing. Therefore, we propose a new regulariza-tion method to encourage diverse sampling in conditionalsynthesis. In addition, we propose a feature pyramid dis-criminator to improve the image quality. Our experimen-tal results show that our model can produce more diverseimages without sacrificing visual quality compared to state-of-the-arts approaches in both the CelebA face dataset and the Cityscape scene dataset.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of generating semantically coherent and visually plausible image content in missing or masked regions, while preserving the overall structure and context of the original image. Building on recent advances in adversarial learning, contextual feature encoding, and probabilistic modeling, we propose a novel framework that integrates contextual awareness with generative capabilities to achieve high-quality image inpainting. Our approach leverages a multi-stage adversarial training process that explicitly incorporates contextual information from the surrounding image regions to guide the synthesis of missing content. By combining the strengths of feature-based inpainting and probabilistic modeling, our method is capable of generating structurally accurate and visually realistic results, even for large missing regions. We demonstrate that our framework outperforms existing methods in terms of both structural coherence and photorealism, as measured by standard evaluation metrics. Our results suggest that integrating contextual and adversarial learning can significantly enhance the quality of image inpainting, opening new possibilities for applications in image editing, restoration, and scene completion.

original_abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) is one of the best methods for understanding the differences in semantic rules between two languages. Especially for Indo-European languages, subword-level models have achieved impressive results. However, when the translation task involves Chinese, semantic granularity remains at the word and character level, so there is still need more fine-grained translation model of Chinese. In this paper, we introduce a simple and effective method for Chinese translation at the sub-character level. Our approach uses the Wubi method to translate Chinese into English; byte-pair encoding (BPE) is then applied. Our method for Chinese-English translation eliminates the need for a complicated word segmentation algorithm during preprocessing. Furthermore, our method allows for sub-character-level neural translation based on recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture, without preprocessing. The empirical results show that for Chinese-English translation tasks, our sub-character-level model has a comparable BLEU score to the subword model, despite having a much smaller vocabulary. Additionally, the small vocabulary is highly advantageous for NMT model compression.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of achieving robust and efficient open-vocabulary neural machine translation (NMT) across diverse language pairs, particularly those involving morphologically rich and structurally dissimilar languages. Building on prior work that explores subword units, character-level modeling, and hybrid approaches, we propose a novel architecture that integrates the strengths of word-level and character-level representations. Our model operates primarily at the word level, leveraging the efficiency and accuracy of word-based systems, while incorporating character-level components to handle rare and unseen words. This hybrid design avoids the pitfalls of both purely word-based and fully character-based models, such as the generation of unknown words or excessive computational overhead. We demonstrate that this approach improves translation quality on multiple language pairs, including those with complex morphological structures, without requiring explicit segmentation or extensive preprocessing. Our experiments show that the proposed method achieves competitive performance on standard benchmarks, offering a practical and scalable solution for open-vocabulary NMT.

original_abstract: While cutting-edge image captioning systems are increasingly describing an image coherently and exactly, recent progresses in continual learning allow deep learning systems to avoid catastrophic forgetting. However, the domain where image captioning working with continual learning is not exploited yet. We define the task in which we consolidate continual learning and image captioning as continual image captioning. In this work, we propose ContCap, a framework continually generating captions over a series of new tasks coming, seamlessly integrating continual learning into image captioning accompanied by tackling catastrophic forgetting. After proving catastrophic forgetting in image captioning, we employ freezing, knowledge distillation, and pseudo-labeling techniques to overcome the forgetting dilemma with the baseline is a simple fine-tuning scheme. We split MS-COCO 2014 dataset to perform experiments on incremental tasks without revisiting dataset of previously provided tasks. The experiments are designed to increase the degree of catastrophic forgetting and appraise the capacity of approaches. Experimental results show remarkable improvements in the performance on the old tasks, while the figure for the new task remains almost the same compared to fine-tuning. For example, pseudo-labeling increases CIDEr from 0.287 to 0.576 on the old task and 0.686 down to 0.657 BLEU1 on the new task.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of enabling deep neural networks to incrementally learn new tasks without catastrophic forgetting, a phenomenon where performance on previously learned tasks degrades when new tasks are introduced. Building on prior work that explores methods for continual learning, such as distillation-based approaches, rehearsal strategies, and architectural modifications, we propose a novel framework that integrates knowledge retention mechanisms with efficient adaptation to new classes. Our approach leverages a combination of distillation loss and task-specific regularization to maintain performance on old tasks while learning new ones. We design a method that operates without requiring access to the original training data, relying instead on a small set of exemplars and a frozen copy of the previous model to guide the learning process. The framework is evaluated on standard image classification and semantic segmentation benchmarks, demonstrating its effectiveness in maintaining performance across multiple incremental learning steps. Our results indicate that the proposed method achieves a favorable balance between computational efficiency and retention of previously learned knowledge, offering a promising direction for scalable and practical continual learning systems.

original_abstract: Recent advancements in machine learning research, i.e., deep learning, introduced methods that excel conventional algorithms as well as humans in several complex tasks, ranging from detection of objects in images and speech recognition to playing difficult strategic games. However, the current methodology of machine learning research and consequently, implementations of the real-world applications of such algorithms, seems to have a recurring HARKing (Hypothesizing After the Results are Known) issue. In this work, we elaborate on the algorithmic, economic and social reasons and consequences of this phenomenon. We present examples from current common practices of conducting machine learning research (e.g. avoidance of reporting negative results) and failure of generalization ability of the proposed algorithms and datasets in actual real-life usage. Furthermore, a potential future trajectory of machine learning research and development from the perspective of accountable, unbiased, ethical and privacy-aware algorithmic decision making is discussed. We would like to emphasize that with this discussion we neither claim to provide an exhaustive argumentation nor blame any specific institution or individual on the raised issues. This is simply a discussion put forth by us, insiders of the machine learning field, reflecting on us.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of designing effective neural network architectures with minimal human intervention, building on prior work that explores reinforcement learning, evolutionary algorithms, and random search strategies for automated architecture discovery. While existing methods have demonstrated impressive performance on benchmark datasets, they often lack rigorous evaluation of their search processes and may not consistently outperform simpler baselines. We propose a systematic evaluation framework that assesses the quality of candidate architectures during the search phase, rather than relying solely on final validation performance. Our analysis reveals that current search strategies, including state-of-the-art NAS algorithms, do not reliably outperform random selection and that weight sharing can distort the evaluation of candidate architectures. These findings highlight the need for more robust and transparent NAS methodologies that ensure the search process effectively identifies high-performing architectures. We conclude that future research should focus on improving the evaluation of search strategies to ensure that discovered architectures are not only accurate but also reliably superior to alternatives.

original_abstract: One of the primary challenges faced by deep learning is the degree to which current methods exploit superficial statistics and dataset bias, rather than learning to generalise over the specific representations they have experienced. This is a critical concern because generalisation enables robust reasoning over unseen data, whereas leveraging superficial statistics is fragile to even small changes in data distribution. To illuminate the issue and drive progress towards a solution, we propose a test that explicitly evaluates abstract reasoning over visual data. We introduce a large-scale benchmark of visual questions that involve operations fundamental to many high-level vision tasks, such as comparisons of counts and logical operations on complex visual properties. The benchmark directly measures a method's ability to infer high-level relationships and to generalise them over image-based concepts. It includes multiple training/test splits that require controlled levels of generalization. We evaluate a range of deep learning architectures, and find that existing models, including those popular for vision-and-language tasks, are unable to solve seemingly-simple instances. Models using relational networks fare better but leave substantial room for improvement.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of enabling models to answer questions about images with reasoning capabilities that go beyond the scope of their training data. While prior work has focused on improving performance on standard benchmarks and incorporating structured representations, these approaches often fail to generalize to novel questions or images. We propose a method that leverages meta learning to enable models to reason about new questions using dynamically provided support examples. By adapting state-of-the-art VQA models with techniques from the meta learning literature, our approach allows the system to generate answers that were not seen during training. This represents a significant step toward models that can learn and reason on-the-fly, rather than relying solely on pre-learned knowledge. Our experiments demonstrate that this method achieves higher recall of rare answers and better sample efficiency compared to existing approaches, highlighting its potential for more flexible and robust vision-and-language systems.

original_abstract: In this paper, we propose a Dual Focal Loss (DFL) function, as a replacement for the standard cross entropy (CE) function to achieve a better treatment of the unbalanced classes in a dataset. Our DFL method is an improvement on the recently reported Focal Loss (FL) cross-entropy function, which proposes a scaling method that puts more weight on the examples that are difficult to classify over those that are easy. However, the scaling parameter of FL is empirically set, which is problem-dependent. In addition, like other CE variants, FL only focuses on the loss of true classes. Therefore, no loss feedback is gained from the false classes. Although focusing only on true examples increases probability on true classes and correspondingly reduces probability on false classes due to the nature of the softmax function, it does not achieve the best convergence due to avoidance of the loss on false classes. Our DFL method improves on the simple FL in two ways. Firstly, it takes the idea of FL to focus more on difficult examples than the easy ones, but evaluates loss on both true and negative classes with equal importance. Secondly, the scaling parameter of DFL has been made learnable so that it can tune itself by backpropagation rather than being dependent on manual tuning. In this way, our proposed DFL method offers an auto-tunable loss function that can reduce the class imbalance effect as well as put more focus on both true difficult examples and negative easy examples. Experimental results show that our proposed method provides better accuracy in every test run conducted over a variety of different network models and datasets.
generated_abstract: In this paper, we address the challenge of accurate and efficient brain tumor segmentation in magnetic resonance (MR) images, a task complicated by the variability in tumor shape, size, and contrast. Building on prior work that explores deep neural networks and fully convolutional architectures for semantic segmentation, we propose a novel approach that integrates advanced network design with effective training strategies to improve segmentation performance while maintaining computational efficiency. Our method leverages hierarchical feature learning and incorporates a refined loss function to address class imbalance, a common issue in medical image segmentation. We adapt encoder-decoder structures with atrous separable convolutions and explore multi-scale contextual information to enhance boundary detection. Additionally, we introduce a two-phase training procedure to better handle the distribution of tumor labels. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves competitive performance on benchmark datasets, offering a more robust and efficient solution for brain tumor segmentation.

original_abstract: Given an artistic portrait, recovering the latent photorealistic face that preserves the subject’s identity is challenging because the facial details are often distorted or fully lost in artistic portraits. We develop an Identity-preserving Face Recovery from Portraits method that utilizes a Style Removal network (SRN) and a Discriminative Network (DN). Our SRN, composed of an autoencoder with residual block-embedded skip connections, is designed to transfer feature maps of stylized images to the feature maps of the corresponding photorealistic faces. Owing to the Spatial Transformer Network, SRN automatically compensates for misalignments of stylized portraits to output aligned realistic face images. To ensure the identity preservation, we promote the recovered and ground truth faces to share similar visual features via a distance measure which compares features of recovered and ground truth faces extracted from a pre-trained FaceNet network. DN has multiple convolutional and fully-connected layers, and its role is to enforce recovered faces to be similar to authentic faces. Thus, we can recover high-quality photorealistic faces from unaligned portraits while preserving the identity of the face in an image. By conducting extensive evaluations on a large-scale synthesized dataset and a hand-drawn sketch dataset, we demonstrate that our method achieves superior face recovery and attains state-of-the-art results. In addition, our method can recover photorealistic faces from unseen stylized portraits, artistic paintings, and hand-drawn sketches.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of achieving high-quality, controllable, and efficient artistic style transfer that preserves content structure while adapting to arbitrary styles. Building on prior work that leverages convolutional neural networks for style transfer, we observe that existing methods often struggle with balancing speed, flexibility, and visual fidelity. We propose a novel approach that integrates perceptual loss functions with adaptive normalization techniques to enable real-time style transfer without predefining a set of styles. Our method allows for fine-grained control over the content-style balance, spatial distribution, and color characteristics, enhancing the robustness and versatility of the stylization process. By combining the strengths of optimization-based and feed-forward approaches, we achieve results that are both visually appealing and computationally efficient. We demonstrate that our framework improves upon previous methods in terms of convergence speed, stability, and user control, while maintaining compatibility with a wide range of content and style inputs. Our experiments confirm that the proposed approach effectively addresses common failure cases and offers a more flexible and reliable solution for artistic style transfer.

original_abstract: Quantization of neural networks has become common practice, driven by the need for efficient implementations of deep neural networks on embedded devices. In this paper, we exploit an oft-overlooked degree of freedom in most networks - for a given layer, individual output channels can be scaled by any factor provided that the corresponding weights of the next layer are inversely scaled. Therefore, a given network has many factorizations which change the weights of the network without changing its function. We present a conceptually simple and easy to implement method that uses this property and show that proper factorizations significantly decrease the degradation caused by quantization. We show improvement on a wide variety of networks and achieve state-of-the-art degradation results for MobileNets. While our focus is on quantization, this type of factorization is applicable to other domains such as network-pruning, neural nets regularization and network interpretability.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of deploying deep neural networks on resource-constrained hardware by exploring the feasibility of low-precision training and inference without significant accuracy degradation. Building on prior work that demonstrates the viability of low-precision fixed-point arithmetic and quantization techniques, we investigate how to maintain model performance while reducing computational and memory demands. We propose a method that integrates quantization-aware training with adaptive precision allocation across network layers, enabling the use of low-bit representations during both training and inference. Our approach leverages insights from previous studies on stochastic rounding, weight partitioning, and gradient noise mitigation to ensure robustness in low-precision settings. By carefully balancing quantization-induced errors with training dynamics, we aim to achieve high accuracy with minimal resource overhead. Experimental results on standard benchmarks indicate that our method enables effective deployment of deep networks using low-precision arithmetic, demonstrating that accurate inference is achievable with significantly reduced computational and memory requirements. These findings contribute to the ongoing effort to make deep learning more accessible on embedded and mobile platforms.

original_abstract: We propose a planning and perception mechanism for a robot (agent), that can only observe the underlying environment partially, in order to solve an image classification problem. A three-layer architecture is suggested that consists of a meta-layer that decides the intermediate goals, an action-layer that selects local actions as the agent navigates towards a goal, and a classification-layer that evaluates the reward and makes a prediction. We design and implement these layers using deep reinforcement learning. A generalized policy gradient algorithm is utilized to learn the parameters of these layers to maximize the expected reward. Our proposed methodology is tested on the MNIST dataset of handwritten digits, which provides us with a level of explainability while interpreting the agent's intermediate goals and course of action.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of improving the efficiency and accuracy of deep learning models in complex visual recognition tasks by exploring novel architectures that enhance feature propagation and reduce overfitting. Building on recent advances in deep network structures, we investigate methods to improve local modeling and global feature integration. We propose a new architecture that combines the strengths of dense connectivity and micro network abstraction to better capture hierarchical and spatial dependencies in visual data. Our approach leverages the dense connections to facilitate gradient flow and feature reuse while incorporating micro networks to enhance the discriminative power of local features. We demonstrate that this integration leads to improved performance on standard benchmark datasets. Our experiments show that the proposed method achieves competitive results while maintaining computational efficiency. The findings suggest that combining dense connectivity with enhanced local modeling can lead to more robust and interpretable deep learning models for visual recognition tasks.

original_abstract: While adversarial games have been well studied in various board games and electronic sports games, etc., such adversarial games remain a nearly blank field in natural language processing. As natural language is inherently an interactive game, we propose a challenging pragmatics game called Adversarial Taboo, in which an attacker and a defender compete with each other through sequential natural language interactions. The attacker is tasked with inducing the defender to speak a target word invisible to the defender, while the defender is tasked with detecting the target word before being induced by the attacker. In Adversarial Taboo, a successful attacker must hide its intention and subtly induce the defender, while a competitive defender must be cautious with its utterances and infer the intention of the attacker. To instantiate the game, we create a game environment and a competition platform. Sufficient pilot experiments and empirical studies on several baseline attack and defense strategies show promising and interesting results. Based on the analysis on the game and experiments, we discuss multiple promising directions for future research.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of generating engaging, contextually appropriate, and diverse responses in open-domain dialogue systems. While prior work has demonstrated the potential of generative models and reinforcement learning for dialogue, these approaches often fail to balance coherence, informativity, and long-term engagement effectively. We build on recent advances in hierarchical neural architectures, diversity-promoting objective functions, and multi-agent communication frameworks to propose a novel approach that integrates pragmatic reasoning, strategic dialogue planning, and knowledge-grounded response generation. Our model incorporates mechanisms for bootstrapping from external knowledge sources, simulating future dialogue outcomes, and optimizing for both immediate and long-term conversational success. Through extensive evaluation, we demonstrate that our approach generates more natural, varied, and goal-oriented responses compared to existing methods, while maintaining fluency and coherence. These results suggest that combining pragmatic inference, strategic planning, and knowledge integration is a promising direction for improving the quality and effectiveness of dialogue systems.

original_abstract: This paper presents a new model for visual dialog, Recurrent Dual Attention Network (ReDAN), using multi-step reasoning to answer a series of questions about an image. In each question-answering turn of a dialog, ReDAN infers the answer progressively through multiple reasoning steps. In each step of the reasoning process, the semantic representation of the question is updated based on the image and the previous dialog history, and the recurrently-refined representation is used for further reasoning in the subsequent step. On the VisDial v1.0 dataset, the proposed ReDAN model achieves a new state-of-the-art of 64.47% NDCG score. Visualization on the reasoning process further demonstrates that ReDAN can locate context-relevant visual and textual clues via iterative refinement, which can lead to the correct answer step-by-step.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of maintaining coherent and contextually accurate dialogues in visual dialog systems, where an agent must answer a sequence of questions grounded in an image while considering the history of the conversation. Building on prior work that leverages attention mechanisms and memory-based models for visual reference resolution and question answering, we propose a novel framework that integrates the role of answers more explicitly into the reasoning process. Our approach extends traditional one-stage methods by introducing a two-stage mechanism: first, candidate answers are scored based on their relevance to the image and question, and then, the most promising answers are re-ranked by synergizing with the image and question context. This allows the model to better capture the interplay between visual content, dialog history, and answer relevance. Experiments on the Visual Dialog v1.0 dataset demonstrate that our method achieves a new state-of-the-art performance in normalized discounted cumulative gain, highlighting the importance of incorporating answer information in visual dialog systems.

original_abstract: Retrieve-and-edit based approaches to structured prediction, where structures associated with retrieved neighbors are edited to form new structures, have recently attracted increased interest. However, much recent work merely conditions on retrieved structures (e.g., in a sequence-to-sequence framework), rather than explicitly manipulating them. We show we can perform accurate sequence labeling by explicitly (and only) copying labels from retrieved neighbors. Moreover, because this copying is label-agnostic, we can achieve impressive performance in zero-shot sequence-labeling tasks. We additionally consider a dynamic programming approach to sequence labeling in the presence of retrieved neighbors, which allows for controlling the number of distinct (copied) segments used to form a prediction, and leads to both more interpretable and accurate predictions.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of improving sequence labeling performance in low-resource and cross-lingual settings by leveraging pre-trained contextual representations and transfer learning. Building on recent advances in end-to-end sequence labeling and contextualized word representations, we propose a framework that integrates pre-trained language models with task-specific sequence tagging architectures. Our approach utilizes deep bidirectional representations that capture both syntactic and semantic information, while also enabling effective knowledge transfer across domains and languages. By combining these representations with hierarchical recurrent networks, we aim to reduce reliance on task-specific feature engineering and improve performance in scenarios with limited annotated data. We evaluate our method on multiple sequence labeling tasks, demonstrating significant improvements in accuracy and robustness across different languages and domains. Our results indicate that the proposed framework effectively leverages pre-trained representations to enhance sequence labeling performance, particularly in low-resource and cross-lingual settings.

original_abstract: We present a comprehensive analysis of how and why face recognition accuracy differs between men and women. We show that accuracy is lower for women due to the combination of (1) the impostor distribution for women having a skew toward higher similarity scores, and (2) the genuine distribution for women having a skew toward lower similarity scores. We show that this phenomenon of the impostor and genuine distributions for women shifting closer towards each other is general across datasets of African-American, Caucasian, and Asian faces. We show that the distribution of facial expressions may differ between male/female, but that the accuracy difference persists for image subsets rated confidently as neutral expression. The accuracy difference also persists for image subsets rated as close to zero pitch angle. Even when removing images with forehead partially occluded by hair/hat, the same impostor/genuine accuracy difference persists. We show that the female genuine distribution improves when only female images without facial cosmetics are used, but that the female impostor distribution also degrades at the same time. Lastly, we show that the accuracy difference persists even if a state-of-the-art deep learning method is trained from scratch using training data explicitly balanced between male and female images and subjects.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of improving discriminative feature learning for face recognition under varying conditions such as pose, age, and illumination. Building on recent advances in loss function design and large-scale face datasets, we propose a novel approach that enhances the angular margin in the feature space to achieve better inter-class separation and intra-class compactness. Our method is inspired by the geometric interpretation of face features on a hypersphere, leveraging the insights from existing angular margin losses while addressing limitations in handling covariates that affect recognition performance. We incorporate a refined margin mechanism that adapts to the distribution of face features, aiming to maximize decision margins in angular space while maintaining robustness across diverse conditions. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves improved recognition accuracy, particularly in challenging scenarios involving age and pose variations. Our results suggest that the proposed method effectively mitigates covariate effects, contributing to more reliable and generalizable face recognition systems.

original_abstract: We propose an unsupervised strategy for the selection of justification sentences for multi-hop question answering (QA) that (a) maximizes the relevance of the selected sentences, (b) minimizes the overlap between the selected facts, and (c) maximizes the coverage of both question and answer. This unsupervised sentence selection method can be coupled with any supervised QA approach. We show that the sentences selected by our method improve the performance of a state-of-the-art supervised QA model on two multi-hop QA datasets: AI2's Reasoning Challenge (ARC) and Multi-Sentence Reading Comprehension (MultiRC). We obtain new state-of-the-art performance on both datasets among approaches that do not use external resources for training the QA system: 56.82\% F1 on ARC (41.24\% on Challenge and 64.49\% on Easy) and 26.1\% EM0 on MultiRC. Our justification sentences have higher quality than the justifications selected by a strong information retrieval baseline, e.g., by 5.4\% F1 in MultiRC. We also show that our unsupervised selection of justification sentences is more stable across domains than a state-of-the-art supervised sentence selection method.
generated_abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of answering complex questions that require integrating information from multiple, disjoint sources. While prior work has focused on single-document or single-sentence reasoning, we extend the task to scenarios where answers must be derived through multi-step inference across multiple documents. Building on recent advances in multi-passage reading comprehension and multi-hop reasoning, we propose a novel framework that combines evidence aggregation with cross-passage verification to improve answer accuracy. Our approach leverages existing methods for passage retrieval and answer extraction, but introduces a structured mechanism to evaluate and combine evidence from multiple sources. We demonstrate that this method significantly improves performance on multi-hop question answering tasks by reducing the impact of noisy or conflicting information. Our experiments show that the proposed approach outperforms existing models on standard benchmarks, highlighting the importance of cross-source reasoning in open-domain question answering. The results suggest that integrating evidence from multiple documents is essential for handling complex, real-world questions.
